narrative:
The model predicted a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) for both Year 1 and Year 3, far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 30.5 worked in the opposite direction, modestly pulling the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your academic rankings. Other details such as your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 (nearly identical to the accepted average), upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time were much less influential.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Targeted preparation in these areas could meaningfully change how a similar model evaluates your next application. (218 words)
